routes.description: Establish a cumulative historical route from early Pauline bodily-resurrection testimony through transmitted Gospel and external witness evidence to an identifiable, structured apostolic community continuous with Catholic Christianity.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the early sources warrant bodily rather than merely visionary resurrection belief, the transmission and external evidence remain historically usable, and institutional and doctrinal continuities identify a durable apostolic church despite later disputes.

motionBridge.description: Connect convergent resurrection evidence and early ecclesial continuity into a historically credible account of bodily resurrection and Catholic continuity.

centralBridges.description: Show that the earliest Pauline material describes a transformed bodily resurrection and appearances rather than an exclusively internal vision.
Show that Pauline, Gospel, patristic, and hostile-source lines can be historically combined without depending on a single late tradition.
Trace recognizable offices and a substantially stable doctrinal core through early disputes into the ancient apostolic churches.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Use shared councils, fathers, and core doctrines across Roman, Eastern, and Syriac churches as support for a common inheritance.
Distinguish continuity-preserving reform and schism from later developments alleged to constitute substantive doctrinal departure.

routes.description: Establish that the cited sources underdetermine bodily resurrection, that transmission and preservation processes weaken claims of independent corroboration, and that early Christian plurality prevents a secure inference to specifically Catholic continuity.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if visionary and inherited-report explanations remain viable, surviving texts and hostile witnesses cannot securely resolve transmission and selection uncertainty, and diverse early communities defeat a determinate linear path to later Catholic identity.

motionBridge.description: Show that the combined evidence does not sufficiently distinguish bodily resurrection and Catholic continuity from viable skeptical historical alternatives.

centralBridges.description: Show that Paul's experience and reports about other witnesses do not independently establish encounters with a resurrected body.
Show that compositional delay, unidentified sources, copying uncertainty, and selective preservation limit the evidential force of surviving materials.
Show that competing communities and retrospective definitions of orthodoxy obstruct a simple continuity inference from earliest Christianity to Catholicism.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Use differing regional churches and changing historical classifications to test claims of uniform institutional and doctrinal development.
Use pre-Reformation reform and the difficulty of individuating Christian traditions to challenge sharp continuity and departure boundaries.

sections.title: Pauline Evidence for Bodily Resurrection and Appearances
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether the earliest cited Christian writings establish a tangible transformed body and bodily encounters, or remain compatible with visionary experience and inherited witness reports.

sections.title: Gospel Sources and Textual Transmission
sections.rationale: The historical force of Gospel material depends on whether the interval before composition, source identification, authorial selection, copying, and possible interpolation permit reliable access to early testimony.

sections.title: Hostile Witnesses and Documentary Preservation
sections.rationale: External descriptions can contribute independent corroboration only insofar as their identification of Christians and their survival are not materially distorted by interpolation or selective preservation.

sections.title: Early Orthodoxy, Diversity, and Ecclesial Structure
sections.rationale: The continuity burden turns on whether early offices and doctrinal convergence identify a persistent apostolic church or whether competing groups, regional variation, and later conciliar definitions make that identity retrospective.

sections.title: Apostolic Continuity, Reform, and Later Christian Divisions
sections.rationale: Comparisons among Catholic, Orthodox, Syriac, Protestant, and medieval reform traditions test which shared doctrines and institutions evidence continuity and where legitimate reform, schism, branching, or departure should be located.

moves.speaker: William Albrecht
moves.proposition: Paul's early, undisputed letters provide early evidence that he believed Christ underwent a bodily resurrection and appeared to him.
moves.attributionBasis: The opening participant explicitly identifies himself as Catholic and frames the historical case affirmatively before Oppy's response.

response.rationale: This constructive move opens the Pauline route by claiming that the earliest undisputed letters evidence belief in bodily resurrection and an appearance to Paul.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it directly establishes a central evidential premise, though the supporting textual details remain compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is recoverable and carefully limited to early undisputed letters, Paul's belief, and evidential support rather than historical certainty.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker presents the letters as early evidence and acknowledges that their details are not extensively fleshed out.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Early attestation of Paul's belief coherently supports the stated historical premise, with the bodily-reading bridge only partly articulated.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move identifies the undisputed Pauline corpus and its early date, but does not quote or analyze the decisive passages in this span.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the indispensable Pauline bodily-reading bridge and sits near the top of the central-contact tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The selected span advances its affirmative textual claim without developing a meaningful competing interpretation for assessment.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly invokes the early, non-deutero-Pauline corpus, bodily resurrection, and an indicated appearance to Paul.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: Paul's early letters remain compatible with a visionary experience and do not clearly establish a bodily meeting with someone who had died and returned to life.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker directly rejects the preceding Pauline claim, and the dialogue subsequently identifies this skeptical participant as Graham Oppy.

components.text: Whether the early Pauline letters establish a bodily encounter rather than remaining compatible with a vision.

response.rationale: The response directly contests the bodily inference by arguing that the letters are unclear and compatible with a visionary experience rather than two bodies meeting.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the decisive bodily-versus-visionary inference, although it does not supply detailed passage-by-passage exegesis.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between a vision and a bodily meeting is clear, and the claim is explicitly framed as underdetermination rather than disproof.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Repeated statements that the letters are unclear fit the limited conclusion that a visionary alternative remains viable.

charity.alternative: The letters may imply a bodily resurrection and an appearance to Paul.
charity.decisiveQualification: Belief in bodily resurrection does not itself specify that Paul's experience was a bodily meeting.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Compatibility with a vision directly defeats an inference from the letters to a clearly bodily meeting without claiming that vision is proven.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual underdetermination is clear, but the excerpt offers little specific textual analysis demonstrating the claimed Pauline ambiguity.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central Pauline-underdetermination bridge by attacking the character of Paul's reported experience.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response preserves the affirmative reading as possible while fairly isolating what the letters allegedly fail to establish.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly contrasts a vision with meeting someone formerly dead and says the early letters do not support two bodies meeting.

moves.speaker: William Albrecht
moves.proposition: First Corinthians 15 contrasts mortal and spiritual bodies while still describing the resurrected body as tangible and transformed rather than immaterial.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker presents a Catholic affirmative reading, references his own Greek analysis, and is addressed elsewhere in the exchange as William.

components.text: Whether First Corinthians 15 supports a tangible transformed body rather than an immaterial resurrection conception.

response.rationale: The answer invokes First Corinthians 15's mortal-body and spiritual-body contrast to reject an exclusively immaterial reading of resurrection.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly contacts the bodily-content issue, but provides assertion of the reading rather than a full explanation of Paul's terminology.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conclusion is clear, but tangible, real, physical, and spiritual body are grouped without fully distinguishing their meanings.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Saying there is no other way to read the passage exceeds the excerpt's compressed contrast and acknowledged existence of rival readings.

charity.alternative: A spiritual body in First Corinthians 15 may be read as immaterial.
charity.decisiveQualification: The mere contrast between mortal and spiritual bodies does not by itself resolve what physicality Paul intended.

logicalCoherence.rationale: A transformed spiritual body can coherently remain bodily, but the inference to tangibility requires a material semantic bridge left implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: First Corinthians 15 is specifically identified, yet the excerpt supplies neither quotation nor sustained Greek or contextual defense of tangibility.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move squarely addresses the central Pauline bodily-reading bridge through the meaning of the resurrection body.

representationalCharity.rationale: The rival reading is mentioned accurately, but the response dismisses it without addressing its strongest linguistic or contextual basis.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts mortal and spiritual bodies, calls the latter tangible and physical, and acknowledges an immaterial rival interpretation.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: Paul's claims about the five hundred and other witnesses are secondhand reports that could have furnished the interpretive framework through which he understood his own experience.
moves.attributionBasis: The skeptical speaker refers to Paul in the third person, challenges evidential transmission, and continues Oppy's previously established position.

components.text: Whether Paul's reported witnesses independently support the bodily-resurrection interpretation of his own experience.
Whether a bodily resurrection framework could have shaped Paul's interpretation without proving a bodily encounter.

response.rationale: The reply identifies the five hundred and other witnesses as secondhand and explains how inherited reports could frame Paul's interpretation of his experience.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly contacts both the independence of the reports and their proposed relationship to Paul's interpretive framework.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between personal observation, secondhand material, and possible interpretive influence is consistently maintained.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The response says the reports could have influenced Paul and does not claim to demonstrate that this causal account occurred.

charity.alternative: Paul's inherited witness list may preserve genuine independent testimony.
charity.decisiveQualification: Even genuine inherited testimony is not Paul's personal observation and may shape how he reports his experience.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between secondhand reports and personal observation supports a coherent alternative explanation of Paul's interpretive framework.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The witness list is specifically identified, but the causal suggestion about its influence on Paul remains plausible rather than independently evidenced.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central Pauline-underdetermination bridge by limiting the independence of reported witnesses.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response does not allege fabrication and fairly focuses on evidential independence and interpretive mediation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt names the five hundred and other witnesses, labels those reports secondhand, and proposes that they filtered Paul's interpretation.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: Known interpolations create unresolved copying uncertainty for Christian texts whose earlier versions and underlying sources are unavailable for comparison.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker advances the skeptical manuscript-transmission argument immediately before Albrecht answers with manuscript and interpolation examples.

components.text: Whether the particular Pauline bodily reading is reliable despite the absence of earlier versions and underlying sources.

response.rationale: The move raises relevant general copying uncertainty, but it does not connect that uncertainty to a specific textual variant or premise in the selected Pauline argument.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It is issue-bearing contrary material about textual reliability, yet it leaves the targeted Pauline inference substantially unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The general copying problem is clear, though the range of Christian texts and sources to which the concern applies is not delimited.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The argument appropriately frames absent earlier versions as creating a question rather than establishing actual corruption.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Unavailable comparators logically limit verification, although uncertainty alone does not establish unreliable copying in any particular text.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Known interpolation and missing earlier versions support caution, but no representative manuscript example grounds the broader application.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the central transmission-preservation uncertainty bridge, though only at a general methodological level.

representationalCharity.rationale: The excerpt formulates a general evidential limitation without engaging a developed opposing account of particular manuscript stability.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts detectable interpolations where versions survive with texts lacking earlier versions and asks how reliably sources were copied.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: The roughly two-generation interval before Gospel composition leaves uncertain which sources the authors possessed, what those sources contained, and how reliably material was selected and transmitted.
moves.attributionBasis: The skeptical participant initiates a new question about late Gospel dating and develops it until Albrecht begins defending Luke's historical style.

components.text: Whether the Pauline bodily interpretation is undermined by Gospel compositional delay and unknown Gospel sources.

response.rationale: The source criticism is central to Gospel reliability but does not answer the earlier Pauline exegesis; it therefore supplies contrary material without target contact.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It is a relevant transmission objection within the broader case, but it does not engage the selected target's decisive Pauline claim.

precisionFindings.rationale: The temporal interval, unknown sources, source contents, and authorial selection are separately and clearly identified as uncertainties.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker uses the delay to establish questions about reliability rather than asserting that the resulting accounts are necessarily false.

charity.alternative: A Gospel author may responsibly act as a historian despite writing two generations later.
charity.decisiveQualification: Historical intent cannot identify unknown sources or establish how their contents were selected and transmitted.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The interval and unavailable source information coherently limit confidence in transmission without entailing wholesale unreliability.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The approximate delay and specific unknowns are identified, though no concrete Gospel episode tests the alleged selection problem.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly and directly advances the central transmission-preservation uncertainty bridge concerning Gospel composition and sources.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response grants the historian description provisionally and identifies the remaining source-access and selection problem.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt identifies a roughly two-generation interval and specifies uncertainty about sources, their contents, authorial politics, and selection.

moves.speaker: William Albrecht
moves.proposition: Patristic testimony about Gospel sources, together with the earlier Pauline material, permits the Gospel traditions to be used as part of a cumulative early historical case.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly adopts the affirmative Catholic position, invokes church fathers and hostile authors, and is addressed as William at the move's conclusion.

components.text: Whether patristic source testimony and other early lines permit cumulative historical use of the Gospel traditions.
Whether multiple Pauline, patristic, Gospel, and hostile-source lines avoid dependence on one uncertain text.
Whether the earlier Pauline material can contribute to a cumulative case despite mediated reports.

response.rationale: The larger selected move appeals to patristic source testimony, Pauline priority, and hostile witnesses as convergent lines answering source-delay concerns.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts multiple transmission concerns, but the rendered excerpt chiefly shifts toward competing groups and hostile identification rather than documenting source independence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The cumulative proposition is recoverable from the move, but the excerpt does not clearly delimit which fathers, sources, or independent markers do the work.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The asserted cumulative usability outruns the excerpt's sparse documentation of source identity, dating, and independence.

charity.alternative: Competing Christian groups and unknown Gospel sources weaken claims of a single transmitted tradition.
charity.decisiveQualification: Hostile identification and patristic attribution help only if their information is early and sufficiently independent.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Convergence could answer single-source dependence, but the inference requires an independence and dating bridge that remains materially underdeveloped.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move invokes broad source classes and hostile markers without giving representative testimony or defending their independence in the rendered evidence.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attempts the central transmission-witness convergence bridge, even though its execution is evidentially compressed.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response notices competition but largely asks for agreement and does not address the strongest independence qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: The locked proposition identifies patristic, Pauline, Gospel, and hostile-source convergence; the excerpt principally discusses competing groups and hostile markers.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: The first centuries contained numerous competing Christian groups, making preconciliar orthodoxy indeterminate until councils established doctrinal boundaries.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker expressly qualifies his expertise while answering Albrecht's continuity question with the skeptical view consistently associated with Oppy.

components.text: Whether preconciliar evidence identifies one determinate orthodox tradition rather than numerous competing Christian groups.

response.rationale: The reply directly rejects determinate early orthodoxy by asserting extensive competition before councils fixed doctrinal boundaries.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It squarely contacts the identification inference, though it supplies little detail about the actual groups and their relative histories.

precisionFindings.rationale: The temporal and conciliar scope is clear, but orthodox shifts between descriptive prevalence and formally settled doctrine.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker acknowledges limited expertise, yet the categorical claim that nothing was orthodox before councils exceeds the evidence supplied.

charity.alternative: A recognizable proto-orthodox tradition may predate formal conciliar definition.
charity.decisiveQualification: Formal doctrinal settlement is not identical to the prior existence or prevalence of an identifiable tradition.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Competition supports indeterminacy, but equating lack of conciliar definition with absence of any prior orthodoxy is an unsupported conditional.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The claim relies on a general assertion about many groups without representative examples, comparative prevalence, or source documentation.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central early-plurality bridge by challenging determinate preconciliar orthodoxy.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response emphasizes formal settlement but does not address the strongest continuity claim based on preconciliar recognition and prevalence.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly asserts many competing groups for the first centuries and says councils performed the work of fixing orthodoxy.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: The surviving pre-Nicene record may disproportionately preserve the later winners, while contrary materials may have disappeared or been destroyed, obscuring early theological diversity.
moves.attributionBasis: The skeptical speaker answers the request for competing pre-conciliar theologies and frames the historical record through loss and winner-controlled preservation.

components.text: Whether the surviving patristic and documentary record is representative enough to establish early orthodox convergence.

response.rationale: The reply directly attacks representativeness by proposing that winners' materials survived while contrary evidence was lost or destroyed.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the preservation premise clearly, but remains a possibility argument without comparative preservation evidence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposition consistently concerns possible survival bias in the pre-Nicene record and does not assert proven destruction.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The possibility is appropriately qualified, although an intuition about later heresies only weakly supports similar earlier diversity.

charity.alternative: Surviving pre-Nicene evidence may genuinely reflect a prevalent theological core.
charity.decisiveQualification: Survival under later winners can distort frequency, but distortion must be evidenced rather than merely supposed.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Selective survival coherently limits inference from absence, though later diversity does not alone establish equivalent lost earlier diversity.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Loss and destruction are plausible mechanisms, but the move offers no representative case or preservation comparison demonstrating systematic bias.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances central early-plurality concerns by attacking the representativeness of the surviving record.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response identifies the strongest preservation vulnerability while stopping short of showing its magnitude or actual operation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt invokes winners, lost or destroyed evidence, and the perceived implausibility of postconciliar divergence without similar earlier diversity.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: Apparently untampered anti-Christian writings may still be unrepresentative because later Christian manuscript preservation could favor hostile texts whose contents were useful to Christian preservers.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker clarifies that his objection concerns survival rather than textual alteration and extends that explanation through the selection-effect conclusion.

components.text: Whether surviving hostile writings provide representative independent corroboration rather than a Christian-selected documentary sample.

response.rationale: The reply distinguishes textual tampering from survival selection and directly challenges the representativeness of hostile-source corroboration.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive preservation issue, but the selected excerpt only partially renders the proposed selection mechanism and evidence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The selection hypothesis is discernible, but the excerpt is fragmented and does not clearly delimit the pagan writings or selection criteria.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker repeatedly labels the proposal a possible hypothesis and appropriately avoids claiming demonstrated selection.

charity.alternative: Untampered hostile writings may independently corroborate widespread early orthodoxy.
charity.decisiveQualification: Authenticity does not itself establish that the surviving hostile sample is representative.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between alteration and selective survival is valid and directly limits what authenticity alone can establish.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move supplies a coherent hypothesis but no concrete preservation practice or hostile-text comparison supporting its actual operation.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It materially supports central transmission-preservation uncertainty, though its focus on hostile sources is narrower than the full bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response fairly preserves authenticity while isolating the distinct and relevant selection-effect qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly calls the proposal a possible hypothesis and redirects the objection toward selection in surviving pagan evidence.

moves.speaker: William Albrecht
moves.proposition: Christianity need not have been widespread before the councils for its first-century offices and persistent structured form to identify the historical community described by outside observers.
moves.attributionBasis: The response presents Catholic institutional continuity in the first person and then explicitly invites the skeptical interlocutor to assess it.

components.text: Whether limited spread and internal conflict prevent identification of a persistent structured apostolic community.
Whether outside evidence must show widespread Christianity for institutional continuity to remain identifiable.
Whether acknowledged conflict and ugliness defeat continuity of offices across the pre-Nicene period.

response.rationale: The reply reframes the identification issue around persistent first-century offices and structure, while conceding conflict and denying that widespread prevalence is required.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly contacts prevalence and plurality concerns, but the continuity from named offices to specifically Catholic identity remains asserted.

precisionFindings.rationale: The temporal continuity claim is clear, but hierarchical structure and clearly Catholic are not supplied stable distinguishing criteria.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Concessions about conflict are explicit, but the confident Catholic identification exceeds the institutional evidence presented in the excerpt.

charity.alternative: Plural groups and selective records make a linear Catholic identification uncertain.
charity.decisiveQualification: Persistent offices show structured continuity only if those offices and their succession uniquely identify the later Catholic community.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Limited spread need not defeat identity, but persistence of generic offices does not without further criteria establish specifically Catholic continuity.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move names bishops, priests, and deacons and alleges persistence, but supplies no representative chronological evidence or rival comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central apostolic-structure continuity bridge by asserting durable offices and institutional form.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response concedes messiness and limited spread but omits the decisive uniqueness and succession qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt names first-century bishops, priests, and deacons, concedes conflict, and claims continuous structured form through Nicaea.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: Christians initially remained a Jewish sect in Roman classification, while limited knowledge of the diaspora and distinct Syrian churches complicates a simple linear account of Catholic institutional continuity.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker expressly states his limited historical knowledge before offering the Jewish-sect and Syrian-church qualifications characteristic of Oppy's skeptical response.

components.text: Whether early Roman classification and divergent regional churches complicate a simple line to Catholic institutional identity.

response.rationale: The response contacts the continuity claim by invoking early Jewish-sect classification and distinct Syrian churches as complications.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It raises two relevant complications, but neither is developed enough to show how the asserted institutional continuity fails.

precisionFindings.rationale: Jewish sect and Syrian churches are identifiable ideas, but their dates, relevant features, and relationship to Catholic continuity remain underspecified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker expressly acknowledges limited knowledge and presents these facts as complications rather than decisive refutations.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Regional divergence can complicate linear continuity, but Roman classification as Jewish does not itself bear directly on internal ecclesial identity.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The claims are historically specific but undeveloped, and the speaker's admitted limited knowledge leaves the institutional implications largely asserted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It supports the subsidiary divergent-communities bridge, though only through compressed and partly indirect examples.

representationalCharity.rationale: The fragment raises qualifications but does not develop a sufficiently complete opposing institutional account for a meaningful charity test.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt describes Christians as a Jewish sect from the Roman perspective and then points to interesting Syrian churches.

moves.speaker: William Albrecht
moves.proposition: Syriac and Roman churches remained substantially aligned in Trinitarian theology, Christology, and Marian belief despite differences of language and later political division.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker clarifies which Syriac church is meant and argues from joint Christological declarations and shared doctrines using an explicitly Catholic perspective.

components.text: Whether Syriac churches are substantively divergent from Roman Christianity in core theology.

response.rationale: The response directly answers the Syrian-divergence example by identifying shared Trinitarian, Christological, and Marian beliefs.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the decisive divergence claim with several substantive areas of alleged agreement.

precisionFindings.rationale: The doctrinal comparison is clear, though Syriac churches is broader than the particular communities and historical periods actually discussed.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Named agreements support substantial convergence, but virtually the same and not that different compress remaining historical disputes.

charity.alternative: Syriac churches may represent a materially divergent line of Christian development.
charity.decisiveQualification: Modern joint declarations and shared doctrines do not by themselves establish uninterrupted ancient institutional identity.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Multiple shared core doctrines coherently rebut sweeping divergence, though doctrinal agreement does not alone prove historical continuity.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Specific doctrinal topics and joint declarations are named, but dates, documents, and countervailing differences are not examined.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the subsidiary cross-church convergence bridge and sits at the top of that tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response addresses doctrinal difference fairly but does not handle the temporal and institutional qualification central to continuity.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt identifies Trinitarian, Christological, and Marian agreement and mentions joint Christological declarations despite different language.

moves.speaker: William Albrecht
moves.proposition: Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, and Syriac churches share central doctrines and conciliar inheritance, while the papacy remains their principal major institutional division.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker identifies papal authority as the chief Catholic-Orthodox dispute while repeatedly describing Catholic, Orthodox, and Syriac churches as apostolic churches.

components.text: Whether Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, and Syriac churches retain enough shared inheritance to count as apostolic churches.

response.rationale: The reply directly answers regional divergence with shared Christology, seven councils, and a substantial apostolic-church core despite incomplete uniformity.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts shared inheritance and concedes nonuniformity, though the papal and institutional differences remain underdeveloped.

precisionFindings.rationale: The relevant church families, shared conciliar inheritance, and incomplete uniformity are stated with a recoverable scope.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim is limited to substantial commonality and explicitly denies complete uniformity, fitting the evidence invoked.

charity.alternative: Major institutional divisions may prevent treating these churches as one continuous apostolic body.
charity.decisiveQualification: Shared councils and doctrines establish common inheritance more readily than singular institutional identity.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Shared councils and doctrine coherently support common inheritance, while the inference to a unified institutional identity remains bounded.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Seven councils and Christology are concrete supports, but the full doctrinal inventory and principal institutional division are not documented.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly and strongly advances the subsidiary cross-church convergence bridge through shared conciliar inheritance.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response acknowledges incomplete uniformity, but gives less attention to the institutional force of the remaining divisions.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt cites shared Christology, seven councils, substantial commonality, and incomplete uniformity among apostolic churches.

moves.speaker: William Albrecht
moves.proposition: Earlier reform movements retained characteristic Catholic teachings, whereas the Reformation progressively discarded such teachings and became a distinct religious system.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly frames the comparison as the Catholic view and contrasts preserved medieval beliefs with Luther, Calvin, and other Protestant traditions.

components.text: Whether continuity can distinguish internal reform from later substantive doctrinal departure.

response.rationale: The response offers a criterion based on retention versus progressive shedding of characteristic Catholic teachings to distinguish reform from departure.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the broader continuity issue, but only indirectly answers the targeted Jewish-sect and Syrian-divergence considerations.

precisionFindings.rationale: The historical contrast is clear, but reform, shedding, and distinct religious system lack a fully specified threshold.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker uses belief language and acknowledges Luther's possible original intention, but the taxonomy remains only selectively supported.

charity.alternative: The Reformation may be continuity-preserving reform despite rejecting some Catholic doctrines.
charity.decisiveQualification: Doctrinal loss establishes a new religious system only if the retained core and reasons for reform are comparatively assessed.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Retention can distinguish reform from departure, but no principled threshold explains why the listed doctrinal changes create a new system.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Several doctrines and reformers are named, yet the historical comparison is selective and lacks representative treatment of retained beliefs.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the subsidiary reform-boundaries bridge by proposing a doctrinal-retention distinction.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response recognizes reform intentions but defines departure mainly through selected Catholic teachings without testing rival core criteria.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts retained Marian beliefs, purgatory, and prayer for the dead with Reformation-era shedding and acknowledges reform intentions.

moves.speaker: William Albrecht
moves.proposition: Catholic and Orthodox theology remains substantially compatible despite popular hostility, linguistic differences, and disputes over teachings such as purgatory and the Immaculate Conception.
moves.attributionBasis: The response concedes Orthodox hostility toward Catholics but appeals to Orthodox acceptance of disputed doctrines and Catholic recognition of valid apostolic orders.

components.text: Whether major Eastern and Roman theological differences defeat substantive apostolic convergence.

response.rationale: The response counters divergence through examples of Orthodox compatibility with purgatory and the Immaculate Conception and recognition of apostolic orders.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts theological divergence with concrete doctrines, but does not establish how representative the cited Orthodox positions are.

precisionFindings.rationale: The compatibility claim and doctrinal examples are clear, though a lot of Orthodox is not a stable or quantified scope.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker acknowledges hostility and linguistic difference, but broad compatibility rests on unquantified examples.

charity.alternative: Catholic and Orthodox differences may be substantive rather than chiefly linguistic.
charity.decisiveQualification: Some compatible Orthodox views do not establish representative agreement or resolve institutional disputes.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Examples of compatibility support bounded convergence, but they do not warrant generalizing across Orthodox theology without a scope bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Specific disputed doctrines and apostolic orders are mentioned, yet the asserted Orthodox acceptance is undocumented and unquantified.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It materially supports the subsidiary cross-church convergence bridge through examples of theological compatibility.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response concedes hostility and disagreement but understates the representativeness and institutional qualifications.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt invokes Orthodox acceptance of purgatory and the Immaculate Conception, linguistic framing, and apostolic orders.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: Protestant traditions are better classified as branches of Christianity because they share scripture and history with Catholicism, and substantial internal differences do not settle how religions should be individuated.
moves.attributionBasis: Oppy's response develops a comparative taxonomy of Christianity, Judaism, Islam, Buddhism, and Hinduism to explain how shared and distinguishing features classify religions.

components.text: Whether doctrinal differences justify classifying Protestant traditions as a distinct religion rather than Christian branches.
Whether shared scripture and history can ground a broader Christian classification despite internal differences.
Whether perceived magnitude of internal difference supplies a principled rule for individuating religions.
